title: Why early startup growth looks like failure: HubSpot, Balsamiq, ConvertKit and the chaos before traction
summary: Jason Cohen argues the first years of even hugely successful startups are chaotic, slow and indistinguishable from failure. HubSpot ended 2006 with 3 customers and 2007 with 48. Nothing objective reliably separates the winners from the failures, so struggle and doubt prove neither success nor failure.

principles.text: Runaway successes spent their first years in slow, near-invisible growth that looked like failure.
principles.quote: after ending 2006 with just 3 (three!) customers, they ended the next year with only 48. That's less than one per week. For a year.

principles.text: The early days of winners and losers feel identical: the same struggle, uncertainty and mess.
principles.quote: The same struggle, same uncertainty, same near-impossibility, same mess.

principles.text: You can't reliably tell productive chaos from chaos that leads nowhere, and standard analyses don't explain the difference.
principles.quote: what *doesn't* explain it is a "feature comparison chart." Or a SWOT. Or financial metrics. Or social media. Or whether they raised money.

principles.text: Every startup rule has exceptions, even founder-market fit, so treat frameworks as guides, not guarantees.
principles.quote: there are exceptions to everything. I say in that article that there needs to be founder-fit, but the founders of AirBnB weren't experienced in hotels or hospitality

principles.text: Most attempts fail, so persistence guarantees nothing. Still, feeling lost and exhausted doesn't mean you're failing.
principles.quote: These things mean you haven't yet succeeded, but neither do they prove that you're failing.
